Number theory: other than encryption with enormous primes, I don't see how it's useful.

Combinatorics: ???

Calculus: in physics and other places to measure change and stuff

topics.title: 9 Confused: Are some trapezoids parallelograms?
topics.text:
Do trapezoids have EXACTLY one pair of parallel sides, or do they have AT LEAST one pair of parallel sides, so they can be a parallelogram? Parallelograms have EXACTLY TWO pairs of parallel sides. For a long time, I've thought trapezoids have exactly one pair of parallel sides. But I'm not sure if it has to be exactly one, because I've seen some programs saying AT LEAST one pair. If this was the case, all parallelograms would be trapezoids, and some but not all trapezoids are parallelograms. Which one is it? Trapezoids having exactly one pair of parallel sides or at least one pair of parallel sides? The poll question is repeated over and over in this post: Do trapezoids have only one pair of parallel sides or at least one pair? When you see a problem with "trapezoid" in it, hopefully the problem will tell you if they want trapezoids with exactly one pair or at least one pair of parallel sides! Also in the poll above, vote what you think the number of parallel side pairs in a trapezoid is.



Uh @hy2015 Post #2 below are you saying exactly one pair of parallel sides? I can't really tell from the statement "Two parallel sides.)... And I did click on your link and read it carefully. Still couldn't figure out if it meant exactly one pair or not.



In just 12 minutes, 9 people including me voted for exactly one pair, only 1 voted for at least one.

topics.title: Rules of powers
topics.text:
I have some doubts related to numbers involving powers of powers of ...



I know the following exponent rule: b^n^m = b^(n^m) i

How this extends to multiple powers?



Consider the number: 2^2^2^16^0.5

Q1. Can we group powers arbitrarily?

That is if the above number is same as follows:



1. 2^2^2^(16^0.5)

2. 2^2^(2^16)^0.5

3. 2^(2^(2^16))^0.5



Now consider the following power rule: (b^n)^m = b^(nxm)

How this rule extends to multiple powers?

Q2. Can we group multiplications of powers arbitrarily?



That is does the above number is same as following:



1. 2^(2x2x16x0.5)

2. 2^2^(2x16x0.5)

3. 2^(2x2x16)^0.5



How all these group in case of both ^ and x.

topics.title: Probability Question-Where did the logic go wrong?
topics.text:
ProblemThere are $5$ students and $4$ teachers on the school publications committee. A group of $5$ members is being selected at random to attend a workshop on school newspapers. What is the probability that the group attending the workshop will have at least 3 students?




Teacher's SolutionDo casework for where there are $3$, $4$, and $5$ students, respectively. It comes down to $\dfrac{81}{126}$, which can be further simplified to $\dfrac{9}{14}$.




Valid Shortcut?True, for this problem, casework probably doesn't take so long, but if the number of students, teachers, and members increase, it will be a different story. So I tried to take a shortcut using this logic.



The total number of ways to select members is obviously: $\dbinom{9}{5}$

Imagine we "give" $3$ students to the committee first: $\dbinom{5}{3}$,

Next, we still have $2$ members left, with $6$ people to choose from: $\dbinom{6}{2}$



Thus, dfrac{\dbinom{5}{3}\dbinom{6}{2}}{\dbinom{9}{5}}

Which is $\dfrac{150}{126}$...greater than 1!



Where did my logic go wrong for the shortcut. It's late, and it might just be that I'm missing something really stupid. Can someone point out what that is?



Thanks

topics.title: Inscribed and Circumscribed Cones
topics.text:
Can you find anything useful about incones (inscribed cones) and circumcones (circumscribed cones)?

Here is what I have found.

Source: 2010 ARML Local Competition Team Round #7

Question 7: A hexagonal pyramid has a regular hexagon of side length 1 for a base, and its apex is located a distance of side length 1 directly above the center of the hexagon. A sphere inscribed inside the pyramid touches every face of the pyramid. Compute the radius of the inscribed sphere.



My Solution: First note that this sphere is tangent to the incone of the hexagonal pyramid. Then find that the base of the incone is inscribed in the base of the hexagonal prism. Doing some work, we find the radius of the base of the incone is $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and the height of the incone is the same height as the hexagonal prism, 1. Now using methods that are already known, we find the radius of the sphere is $\boxed{\frac{\sqrt{21}-3}{4}}$.



We can use a circumcone to find the radius of a circumscribed sphere.



So, as i said in the beginning, can you find any other types of questions where incones or circumcones are useful?

topics.title: 2009 State Mathcounts
topics.text:
The arithmetic progressions $\{2, 5, 8, 11, \ldots\}$ and $\{3, 10, 17, 24, \ldots \}$ have some common values. What is the largest value less than 500 that they have in common?



Here is a solution I read:

Click to reveal hidden textLet $a$ be a common term. We know that \begin{align*}
a&\equiv 2\pmod 3\\
a&\equiv 3\pmod 7
\end{align*}Congruence $(1)$ means that there exists a non-negative integer such that $a=2+3n$. Substituting this into $(2)$ yields \[2+3n\equiv 3\pmod 7\implies n\equiv 5\pmod 7\]So $n$ has a lower bound of $5$. Then $n\ge 5\implies a=2+3n\ge 17$. $17$ satisfies the original congruences, so it is the smallest common term. Subtracting $17$ from both sides of both congruences gives \begin{align*}
a-17&\equiv -15\equiv 0\pmod 3\nonumber\\
a-17&\equiv -14\equiv 0\pmod 7\nonumber
\end{align*}Since $\gcd(3,7)$, we get $a-17\equiv 0\pmod{3\cdot 7}$, that is, $a\equiv 17\pmod{21}$.



So all common terms must be of the form $17+21m$ for some non-negative integer $m$. Note that any number of the form also satisfies the original congruences. The largest such number less than $500$ is $17+21\cdot 22=\boxed{479}$.




The part I don't understand is where t says: Substituting this into $(2)$ yields \[2+3n\equiv 3\pmod 7\implies n\equiv 5\pmod 7\]

Why is 2+3n mod 7 equal to 5 mod 7? How did the 5 come out?



Thanks!

Hi! For the school year of 2016-2017, I have been one of two to be selected to help coach my middle school math club. I chose to coach the upcoming sixth grade year so I could start off with a clean slate and coach them to be strong. However, I am not sure how to start them off.



I know most sixth graders in my school take prealgebra, so they wouldn't have much algebra and most definitely not geometry background. I have many resources that I could use: I have my notes form advanced mathcounts class, the introduction books, the volume 1 book, the white book, and the mathcounts lectures. I am not sure what I should do to start them off.



I was thinking for seventh grade I could use my notes and maybe for eighth grade use the intro or volume or lectures to go more in depth. I feel like maybe I should give a crash course on algebra and geometry so that they have some background knowledge, but I'm not sure if that's the right idea because I also want to prepare them for Mathcounts. Any ideas would be appreciated!



Thanks, Jeannie
